source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL)
finding: AutoFL lets the model call functions to browse the repo (class coverage, method coverage, snippet, comments) and write a root-cause explanation before naming the faulty method. It beat spectrum and mutation baselines at acc@1 on Defects4J and on Python BugsInPy.
numbers: Method-level acc@1 up 166.7% (GPT-3.5) and 233.3% (GPT-4) over Ochiai on BugsInPy. Defects4J v1.0 353 bugs. Average 5.37 function calls per bug; 16.4 s per run with GPT-3.5; 5 runs about 87 s versus 112 s reported for SBFL.
limits: GPT-3.5 lagged SBFL at acc@3 and acc@5; authors say it has trouble digging deep. GPT-4 fixed that. Single GPT-4 run beat five merged GPT-3.5 runs. 56 of 501 BugsInPy bugs unusable.
agent_relevance: Code gathers coverage; the model only reads and names a suspect. Explanation-first then location is a cheap slot order to copy for G2.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL) - hard bugs get longer search
finding: The model searched longer on bugs where the faulty method is not named in the failing test or stack trace. So tool-using localisation adapts effort to difficulty without being told.
numbers: Hardest bugs (not in test, not in trace) used on average 0.6 more calls on Defects4J and 0.9 more on BugsInPy than easiest. One-way ANOVA p<0.05, Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise t-tests at 0.008. Defects4J: 178 bugs in the hardest cell, 47 easiest.
limits: Effect size is small in absolute calls (under one extra call).
agent_relevance: Search depth may be a usable difficulty signal for an impasse detector; but the gap is small, so do not rely on it alone.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL) - confidence from repeated runs
finding: Agreement across 5 reruns (a confidence value) predicts whether the localisation is right. Confidence can filter out wrong answers.
numbers: Spearman with precision@1: +0.57 (Defects4J), +0.52 (BugsInPy); with reciprocal rank +0.67 and +0.50; with average precision +0.70 and +0.49. All p<0.0001, GPT-3.5, 5 reruns.
limits: Correlation, not calibration. Same model sampled five times, so errors are correlated (see G4). Agreement is a hint, not proof.
agent_relevance: Supports counting votes in code as a weak signal, consistent with G4 (hint, never proof).

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL) - explanation quality
finding: Most model explanations of why a method is faulty are not accurate. Developers still wanted a few good explanations over many.
numbers: 300 explanations from 60 Defects4J bugs hand-rated: 20% accurate, 26.3% contained an inaccurate statement, 46.7% were 'bland' (restated the test). At least one accurate explanation for 56.7% of bugs. 16 developers interviewed; 13 agreed FL without explanation would help.
limits: Two authors rated; small sample of bugs.
agent_relevance: A written rationale is not evidence of a right location. Verify by running, not by reading the rationale (G2, G8).

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL) - Defects4J memorisation check
finding: Authors argue the result is not just memory: the same model with no function interaction (Test-GPT3.5) did worse than with function interaction.
numbers: Test-GPT3.5 baseline below AutoFL at every k on both benchmarks.
limits: An indirect argument only; no test on post-cutoff bugs in this paper.
agent_relevance: Treat Defects4J scores of LLMs as possibly inflated; prefer post-cutoff benchmarks.

source: Search summary (2024) AutoFL original preliminary result
finding: Early AutoFL version found the true bug location as top method in 149 of 353 Defects4J cases using only the failing test.
limits: Taken from a search result snippet, not read in the PDF this session.
agent_relevance: Reference point for how much a failing test alone gives.

source: Qin et al. (2025) AgentFL: Scaling LLM-based Fault Localization to Project-Level Context
finding: A three-step ChatGPT agent (comprehend, navigate, confirm) mimics a human debugger. It localised 157 of 395 Defects4J v1.2.0 bugs at Top-1 with no coverage input.
numbers: Top-1/3/5 = 157/183/187 of 395; 28 more Top-1 than the next LLM approach. Cost 0.074 dollars and 97 s per bug. 98 of 395 bugs returned no suspect (user-study set was 297 pairs). Without Closure it matches GRACE at Top-1 and is 12 below it.
limits: Weak at ranking: 319 of 395 cases return fewer than 3 methods, so Top-3 and Top-5 add little. Learning-based GRACE and DeepFL beat it at Top-3/5.
agent_relevance: Verify-then-return design (it validates, not ranks) suits G2: it commits only to a few suspects.

source: Qin et al. (2025) AgentFL: Scaling LLM-based Fault Localization to Project-Level Context - ablation
finding: Each human-like step matters. Removing test failure analysis hurt most.
numbers: Top-1/3/5: full 157/183/187; w/o TestBehaviorAnalysis 148/174/175; w/o MethodDocEnhancement 133/156/160; w/o TestFailureAnalysis 125/148/152 (a 20% Top-1 drop).
limits: Ablated on the same 395 bugs; ChatGPT only.
agent_relevance: Reading the real failing output first is the biggest single step: matches G2 (revise from real output).

source: Qin et al. (2025) AgentFL: Scaling LLM-based Fault Localization to Project-Level Context - replication discrepancy
finding: A later paper (FlexFL) re-ran AgentFL and got fewer Top-1 hits than the original paper, so published LLM-FL numbers move between papers.
numbers: FlexFL's table: AgentFL Top-1/3/5 = 144/169/173 on its Defects4J v1.2 subset, versus 157/183/187 in the AgentFL paper (different bug subset and model version, so not a clean replication).
limits: Different filtering of bugs and API versions; authors do not call it a failed replication.
agent_relevance: Expect 10-ish percent noise from setup alone when comparing LLM-FL papers.

source: Wu, Li, Zhang, Papadakis, Harman, Liu (2023) Large Language Models in Fault Localisation
finding: ChatGPT-4 given one function plus the failing test and error log beat spectrum, mutation and SmartFL at statement level. Without the error log it was clearly worse.
numbers: Mean Top-1 of 23.13 for ChatGPT-4 with log, 46.9% above SmartFL (195 Defects4J versions, function level). Removing the error log cut Top-1 by 25.6%, the biggest drop of four prompt parts.
limits: Function-level context only. Absolute counts are small. Only ChatGPT-3.5 and 4.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: the run's real error output is the single strongest input for localisation.

source: Wu, Li, Zhang, Papadakis, Harman, Liu (2023) Large Language Models in Fault Localisation - context length
finding: Performance depends heavily on how much code is in the prompt. At class level, ChatGPT-4 fell far behind SmartFL, and when context was narrowed to 5 lines either side, baselines caught up and SBFL/SmartFL beat it at Top-5.
numbers: Class level: 49.9% lower Top-1 than SmartFL (56 classes, 5 programs, long classes dropped). Narrowed: 528 faulty statements in prompts.
limits: Class-level set small and biased to short classes.
agent_relevance: Keep prompts local: narrow to the covered or implicated code first, as code (not model) should do.

source: Wu, Li, Zhang, Papadakis, Harman, Liu (2023) Large Language Models in Fault Localisation - consistency and leakage
finding: Adding dynamic execution info made answers more repeatable. A newer student-code dataset (StuDefects, written after 2022) was used to test leakage and ChatGPT still beat the baseline there.
numbers: Variance of Top-1 averaged 12.00% for ChatGPT-4 with log, the lowest of the ChatGPT variants (variance 0.12 to 0.07 across Top-1 to Top-5). Poor class-level result is cited as evidence against pure memorisation.
limits: StuDefects are small student programs, a different distribution from Defects4J.
agent_relevance: Execution evidence reduces run-to-run noise; relevant for G4 (one model's samples are not independent).

source: Rafi, Kim, Chen, Wang (2025) A Multi-Agent Approach to Fault Localization via Graph-Based Retrieval and Reflexion (LLM4FL)
finding: Three agents with coverage-group division, call-graph code navigation and a Reflexion-style re-ranking loop localised 327 of 675 Defects4J v2.0.0 faults at Top-1.
numbers: Top-1/3/5/10 = 327/425/473/494. Versus AutoFL +18.55% and AgentFL/SoapFL +4.82% Top-1. DepGraph (non-LLM learning) still higher at Top-1: 359.
limits: Authors report these as relative gains over reported numbers, not independent re-runs.
agent_relevance: Shows SBFL-ordered coverage split into groups is a good place for code to carve the problem.

source: Rafi, Kim, Chen, Wang (2025) A Multi-Agent Approach to Fault Localization via Graph-Based Retrieval and Reflexion (LLM4FL) - ablation
finding: Dividing the coverage into sorted groups mattered most; the self-reflection re-ranking helped least but still helped.
limits: Reflexion here had no ground-truth feedback, only the model's own re-rank.
agent_relevance: Self-reflection with no new real output gives the smallest gain, consistent with G1/G2.

source: Rafi, Kim, Chen, Wang (2025) A Multi-Agent Approach to Fault Localization via Graph-Based Retrieval and Reflexion (LLM4FL) - spectrum baseline gap
finding: Plain SBFL is far behind LLM agents at Top-1 in this setup, but the gap shrinks at Top-10.
numbers: First baseline row Top-1 121 vs LLM4FL 327 (+169%); Top-10 413 vs 494 (+20%).
limits: Baseline row identity (SBFL) inferred from the table layout in PDF text; setup is 675 faults.
agent_relevance: SBFL is a cheap, useful ordering to feed the model; it is not obsolete as a pre-filter.

source: Xu, Liu, Ren, Zhang, Liang, Lo (2025) FlexFL: Flexible and Effective Fault Localization with Open-Source LLMs
finding: A two-stage design (non-LLM tools shrink the candidate list, then an LLM agent double-checks) lets a small open model (Llama3-8B) beat GPT-3.5 agents.
numbers: FlexFL Top-1/3/5 = 350/478/529 on Defects4J v2.0.0. Llama3-8B version found 42 and 63 more bugs than AutoFL and AgentFL (both GPT-3.5). On a v1.2 subset FlexFL 164/214/236 vs Ochiai 122/192/218, DStar 125/195/216, AgentFL 144/169/173, AutoFL-GPT-3.5 146/180/194.
limits: Authors' own system compared with re-run baselines; AutoFL had to be adapted to Llama3-8B.
agent_relevance: Hybrid code-then-model beats model alone, matching the schema's split of roles (program decides, model fills slots).

source: Xu, Liu, Ren, Zhang, Liang, Lo (2025) FlexFL: Flexible and Effective Fault Localization with Open-Source LLMs - contamination test and over-confident exits
finding: On 28 recent GHRB bugs the model had not seen, FlexFL still worked. GPT-3.5 stopped searching earlier than Llama3-8B, losing precision.
numbers: 19 of 28 GHRB bugs at Top-1 (67.9%) versus 41.9% on Defects4J v2.0.0. Second-stage function calls: 2.82 (GPT-3.5) vs 4.56 (Llama3-8B); Llama3-8B located 39 bugs at Top-1 that GPT-3.5 missed.
limits: Only 28 bugs; GHRB subset has different project mix.
agent_relevance: Confident models quit evidence gathering too soon; a code-side minimum-evidence rule could help (G2).

source: Ji, Lee, Lee, Im, Han (2024) Impact of Large Language Models of Code on Fault Localization
finding: Fine-tuning code LLMs (13 models, 7 architectures) to name the faulty line with no test or coverage input beat learning-based FL on Defects4J line-level.
numbers: UniXcoder pinpointed 653.3 (50.6%), 828.6 (64.2%), 933.3 (72.3%) of 1,291 methods' faults at Top-1/3/5. Up to 1.35x, 1.12x, 1.08x the best learning-based SOTA. Model size did not help (CodeT5 60M and 215M about equal, 710M slightly worse).
limits: Method-level scope with known buggy function; train set (Recoder) may overlap benchmark projects; fine-tuned, not prompted.
agent_relevance: Small fine-tuned encoder-decoder can match big prompted models on single-function FL, but this is out of scope for a no-training scaffold.

source: Yang, Le Goues, Martins, Hellendoorn (2024) Large Language Models for Test-Free Fault Localization (LLMAO)
finding: LLMAO adds small bidirectional adapters to a code LLM to score each line as buggy without any tests. It beat Ochiai and deep-learning FL at Top-1.
numbers: Detects 48 more faults at Top-1 than Ochiai (84.8% improvement), 35.6% over DeepFL, 14.4% over TRANSFER-FL; Top-3 and Top-5 gains smaller. Trained on 350M to 16B models.
limits: Line level on bug-fix sets; needs training; trained and tested on related data. Some column mapping from PDF text is approximate.
agent_relevance: Test-free scoring is possible but weaker than evidence-driven localisation; our agent has tests, so it should use them.

source: Bouzenia, Devanbu, Pradel (2024/2025) RepairAgent: An Autonomous, LLM-Based Agent for Program Repair
finding: A GPT-3.5 agent with a finite state machine (understand, collect ingredients, validate) and tools (search, read, run tests, run FL) fixed 164 Defects4J bugs.
numbers: 164 bugs fixed incl. 39 no baseline fixed; Defects4J v2: 90 vs ChatRepair 48. 270,000 tokens (14 cents) per bug; 35 tool calls per bug. GitBug-Java: 19 plausible, 13 correct, only 4 of 81 multi-line/multi-file bugs.
limits: Default setup gives perfect fault localisation; weaker on multi-line and multi-file bugs.
agent_relevance: The state machine is the same idea as code-driven states in our schema; evidence that code-guided order beats free choice.

source: Bouzenia, Devanbu, Pradel (2024/2025) RepairAgent: An Autonomous, LLM-Based Agent for Program Repair - ablation
finding: On 100 random bugs (full agent fixes 21), removing search tools halved fixes and doubled cost; removing the state machine cut fixes and raised cost; removing long-term memory caused repeated queries.
numbers: Full 21 bugs; no search tools about half; no state machine fewer and costlier; memory off led to repeated commands and wrong file names.
limits: Ablation on 100 bugs only because of budget.
agent_relevance: State machine and no-repeat memory both help: supports code-owned control flow.

source: Bouzenia, Devanbu, Pradel (2024/2025) RepairAgent: An Autonomous, LLM-Based Agent for Program Repair - realistic fault localisation
finding: Replacing perfect fault localisation with a real spectrum tool (GZoltar) cost the agent a quarter of its fixes and nearly doubled the price.
numbers: 16 bugs fixed at 29 dollars instead of 21: a 25% drop in fixes and 81% rise in cost; no extra cycles were allowed.
limits: Same 100-bug subset; GZoltar scores only.
agent_relevance: Many repair numbers assume perfect FL; real localisation is the bottleneck. Repair accuracy cannot be separated from G2 localisation.

source: Xia, Zhang (2024) Keep the Conversation Going: Fixing 162 out of 337 bugs for $0.42 each using ChatGPT (ChatRepair)
finding: Feeding the failing test name, error message and failing line back to ChatGPT in a conversation fixed more bugs than resampling the same prompt.
numbers: 162 of 337 bugs fixed (114 on Defects4J 1.2, 48 on 2.0; 15 and 17 more than prior best); all QuixBugs bugs. About $0.42 per bug. Feedback variants: base 58 plausible, +test name and message 61, +failing line 62 (tries 23.1 to 21.9, cost $0.071 to $0.061). Conversation length 1 gave fewest plausible; length 3 beat 5 and 6 on cost.
limits: Assumes the perfect fault location is given. Base ChatGPT sampling was slightly worse than CodexRepair on Defects4J 1.2.
agent_relevance: Real failing output fed back is what helps (G2). Short feedback history is enough.

source: Xia, Wei, Zhang (2023) Automated Program Repair in the Era of Large Pre-trained Language Models
finding: Nine code models (125M to 20B) used with no fine-tuning beat all older repair tools on five datasets; larger models fixed more, and suffix code after the bug helped infilling.
numbers: 9 PLMs, 3 repair settings, 5 datasets, 3 languages; Codex fixed 32 more bugs than the best older tool on Defects4J 1.2 (per paper intro).
limits: Fault location is given in all settings (infilling and single-line settings need it).
agent_relevance: Repair is easy once the location is known; localisation is the hard step the schema must own.

source: Sobania, Briesch, Hanna, Petke (2023) An Analysis of the Automatic Bug Fixing Performance of ChatGPT
finding: On the 40 Python QuixBugs bugs, ChatGPT fixed about as many as Codex and a deep-learning repair tool; one hint from the failing test raised it a lot.
numbers: 19 of 40 fixed without hints (Codex 21, CoCoNuT 19); 31 of 40 with a single hint (the expected output of the failing test) in the dialogue.
limits: 40 small programs, probably in training data; two ChatGPT versions; hints given by the authors.
agent_relevance: A one-line real test output hint lifts success from 48% to 78%: a small cost to add real evidence (G2).

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents - hierarchical localisation ablation
finding: A fixed three-step localisation (file, then class/function, then edit lines) with no agent loop reached competitive localisation on SWE-bench Lite (300 issues). Giving whole files or going straight to lines was worse.
numbers: File-level hit rate: prompting-based retrieval 78.7%, embedding-based 67.7%, combined 81.7%. Skeleton format beat full file content (cost and hit rate). Direct file-to-line was worse than the hierarchy. Repair: greedy 88 (29.33%), multi-samples 96 (32.00%) at $0.29.
limits: Earlier SWE-bench Lite, GPT-4o; overlaps with the llm_debugging subfolder, only localisation numbers noted here.
agent_relevance: Narrow in code-owned stages: file, element, line. The model never sees more than it needs.

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents - localisation versus repair gap
finding: Good localisation does not guarantee solving: one commercial tool had the top file-level localisation yet a low solve rate. Only 94 of 213 generated reproduction tests were correct after the true patch.
numbers: OpenCSG StarShip file-level 90.0% but solve rate 23.67%. Reproduction tests: 213 of 300 reproduce the issue; only 94 pass with the ground-truth patch.
limits: No trajectories available for the commercial tool, so the gap is unexplained.
agent_relevance: Localisation is necessary, not sufficient; G3 (pass on something not fitted) still needed after G2.

source: Chen, Tang, Deng et al. (2025) LocAgent: Graph-Guided LLM Agents for Code Localization
finding: Parsing the repo into a graph (files, classes, functions, imports, calls, inheritance) lets an agent do multi-hop search. A fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B nearly matched a Claude-3.5 agent at about 86% lower cost.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite file Acc@1/3/5: BM25 38.69/-/61.68; CodeRankEmbed 52.55/77.74/84.67; Agentless GPT-4o 67.15/74.45/74.45; OpenHands Claude-3.5 70.80/84.67/88.32; LocAgent Claude-3.5 75.91/90.51/92.70; fine-tuned Qwen up to 92.7% file Acc@5. Downstream issue resolution up 12% at Pass@10.
limits: Fine-tuned models trained on data like the benchmark; table columns reconstructed from PDF text, so row-to-model mapping is approximate.
agent_relevance: A static call/import graph is code-computed structure the model can query; same role as code locates (G2).

source: Chen, Tang, Deng et al. (2025) LocAgent: Graph-Guided LLM Agents for Code Localization - retrieval vs agent
finding: Embedding retrieval is far behind agents at the exact-function level.
numbers: Function Acc@5: BM25 31.75, E5-base 39.42, Agentless GPT-4o 55.47, MoatlessTools 57.30, OpenHands GPT-4o 68.25 (approximate row mapping).
limits: Single benchmark; GPT-4o and Claude-3.5 only.
agent_relevance: Searching with tools beats one-shot retrieval for fine-grain locating; but search must be structured.
